definition: The degree to which a software product is intuitive, user-friendly, and requires minimal training to operate effectively.
extendedDefinition: Ease of use is how intuitively a software product operates with minimal training, and it is the most cited factor in adoption success and abandonment alike. Easy products get used; complex ones get bypassed in favor of spreadsheets and workarounds, no matter how capable they are. Buyers should evaluate ease of use for the least technical users in the organization, since products designed for administrators or power users often fail in the broader workforce. Task-based trials are the reliable measure: have representative users attempt core workflows without assistance and observe where they stall. Ease of use also has economic weight, because it reduces training investment, support tickets, and rollout time. Trade-offs arise when ease conflicts with depth, so teams should verify that simplicity does not come at the cost of required configuration or control.
examples: A new user completes a common task without coaching and records where labels or navigation cause confusion.
A team compares onboarding time and error rates across two products using the same task list.
A buyer tests whether less-frequent users can find reports and settings after several weeks without daily practice.
description: Ease of use is how readily intended users can complete key tasks; evaluate it with representative users rather than relying only on a vendor demo.
